utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, I did not allow you to ask the question whether a particular response was proportionate, and the reason for that is that that is ultimately a question for the Chamber to decide, being very relevant to the question of self-defence. But there's a difference between the witness giving his view on that question and the witness providing information to the Chamber which will assist it in arriving at its decision. I'm going to allow you to return to that question and to ask the witness to comment on the scale of the attack, the scale of the response, the type of weapons used by both sides, and ultimately even to offer his view as to the proportionality. That is consistent with what I said earlier about the witness providing information that gives us a factual basis on which to make an assessment. So I'm going to allow you to do that, and then of course I will allow the Defence, if it so wishes, to cross-examine on that issue arising from the questions that you ask. Now, let us continue with the cross-examination and proceed as quickly as possible. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I will really do my very best to focus. I've been paring back my question list in order to focus on only what is absolutely essential. I'll try to wrap up my cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Sir Nicolai, you do know that we spoke about several issues yesterday. I broached the subject yesterday which I did not finish. In a way, this has to do with what we have just heard from the President of the Chamber. I would like to quote to you a portion of document D00-0319. This is the statement you provided 10 years after your return from Sarajevo. The event took place four days after your arrival. We find this event described in paragraph 7 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please bring that up for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, as soon as you have it, I would like to quote the paragraph for your benefit. Do you see that? Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say: "When I refer to a quiet period in February and March 1995, I must point out that everything is relative. I recall that on the 27th of February there were over 900 firing incidents in Sarajevo." And then you go on to emphasise: "The figure includes incoming and outgoing shells as well as small-arms fire." I don't want to ask you about who provoked these firing incidents; we talked about that yesterday, and there's evidence to that effect. But does that not mean that it was in fact quite a proportionate affair, 900 shells flying in from one of the sides and 900 shells, or thereabouts, flying in from the other side? That's at least how I read the passage. Please enlighten me if my reading is not correct.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like, indeed, to correct this a little bit. The essentials here are not shells but rounds from small-arms fire. I will not exclude that there were rounds of shells as well, but most of the firing was of small-calibre arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your explanation, sir, but we're talking about mortars. Was that in proportion to, as it were -- of course, small-arms fire is important as well and there will be a lot of references to that throughout this trial. But when we speak about shells, there was some sort of reasonable proportion there, too, the same amount of shells on both sides, roughly speaking. It's difficult to count them in and out, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It is very difficult to make this distinction, particularly when small arms are fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is only rarely that I decide to show video clips that sometimes can elicit certain unpleasant emotions. However, I now find myself compelled to show a video clip. Prior to that I'll be asking the witness a question. It's a very short clip. I might be showing this clip again in its full length, but all we need at this point in time is 30 or 40 seconds of that clip, particular piece of footage. I received this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic. Show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I got it from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska. May that video clip be shown now, please. First I would like to ask the witness to preface the clip. Back in March does he remember something happening that caused a lot of commotion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two young girls were killed at Grbavica. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I vaguely remember the death of two girls. I have to add to this that throughout my entire period there had been numerous cases of civilian casualties, and this, to a certain degree, explains why such a terrible event is not that clear in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, March was a month of cease-fires, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The OTP will help me with the technology. They agreed to show the clip on my behalf. I think it's about to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we play this clip, I wish to register a couple of objections for the record. First of all, I deem the evidence that we are about to see to be, strictly speaking, irrelevant. It is not a defence to any crimes that the defendant, the accused, may have committed, that others committed crimes as well. In addition to that, Your Honour, I would ask Mr. Tapuskovic to let us know, was this disclosed to the OTP before this morning. I do not rule out that it was, but I have no memory of seeing it,. But it was just shown this morning to me and I did not have an opportunity to check any records or chronologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, on the two points, first, the more important one, relevance; and the second, disclosure. Let me hear from you on those two points. And bear in mind, too, the witness's response to you when you were seeking to lay the foundation for showing this clip. He might not be able to help you much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand why you wish to hear me on this. I would not have shown the video clip had the witness not answered the question the way he did. He says he has a foggy recollection of some things. Once I've shown him the video clip, he might be able to tell us better whether he remembers this or not. The relevant thing about it is this happened during a period of cease-fire, and following this incident, tensions mounted again between the clashing sides, the clashing parties. After that, a lot of things actually occurred that are relevant for our purposes regarding the relations between the warring sides. As far as the document's authenticity is concerned, I have a document that I obtained from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska. That's where I obtained the document. Of course, it's necessary to see whether that's authentic, should the OTP be challenging the authenticity of the document. And after that, then, it's down to the Chamber, of course, to evaluate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you must establish is how it impacts on any question of the liability of your client, the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have pointed out on a number of occasions, and now I would have to launch into a lengthy explanation in order to explain the point away, but precious little was known about what went on on the Republika Srpska side and what caused some of their reactions. The Chamber must focus on evidence about that, and I must ask OTP witnesses about these circumstances, too. Unless the Chamber does just that, I think the Chamber will not quite be able to take in the whole picture, the overall context of all these events. It is true that it is not Mr. Milosevic who stands indicted of this particular incident, but this is useful background information which we might use to explain a lot of things that actually went on inside the conflict. We must focus on both sides of the conflict, what went on on the one side and the other, and we must use every witness that can possibly shed light on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any allegation in the indictment which is proximate to this event? Do any of the incidents in the indictment come close in time to the killing of these two girls?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during our Defence case, we shall be introducing a whole lot of evidence. I can't disclose what my defence case will be right now, but once we are conducting our defence case, we shall show the relevance; we shall show what exactly occurred on those days. On the other hand, that precisely is the issue here. There is this attempt to show this to the entire world. The whole video clip speaks about that. There was a great deal of difficulty entailed - I'm not going into that right now - but the world has never seen any of the events shown in this video clip. However, I'm going to be dealing with that during our defence case and offering a whole lot of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that one of your arguments for showing this video clip is to show it to the world?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That is the last thing. Maybe -- absolutely not. Absolutely not. Above all, what I'm trying to do -- I'm telling you, the world has never seen it. It has never leaked through, in manner of speaking. If you wish, we can do this in closed session. I'm not adamant about this, Your Honours. Not at all. You may as well, if you like -- I'm not trying to cause any ill feeling there. You can show it in closed session, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the second point of disclosure, and then we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been four days I've been trying to achieve something with this technology to see if the clip can be shown to the Chamber, yet we have so far failed. It wasn't until a minute ago that the OTP offered to give us a hand, and I'm sure they can show the clip without us wasting time. We've spent the last five days with the technicians trying to have them do that for us, but we have failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. The Chamber will consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the clip to be shown as being relevant to the overall context, but ultimately the weight to be attached to it will depend, of course, on the rest of the evidence. So bear that in mind, Mr. Tapuskovic. Let it be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is no showing on our side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicolai, having seen this video clip, could you perhaps remember this particular incident? What sort of tensions did this trigger in the overall context of events between the warring parties? Was anything going on in those days, or nothing at all, no reaction? First of all, let me ask you, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my regret, I have to admit that this footage has not triggered any additional memories in my mind. I still vaguely recall that there has been an incident of two girls having been killed. However, this memory is so vague that I cannot say anything more in addition to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President. I wasn't going to ask any further questions. I would like to move on to the other document since I must. D00-0287. This is the statement that Mr. Nicolai provided back in 1996. In the English -- this is page 6, the last paragraph of page 6. The B/C/S reference is 6 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that now, sir? This is about the 15th of May; right? I would like to read this out for you. "From about the 15th of May the situation escalated with more firing incidents. For several days in a row in Sarajevo, there been shelling all day long from both sides, and this only stopped in the evenings. Most of the time the shelling had been on military positions. They shelled the BH army barracks by the Zetra stadium, the Tito barracks, the PTT building, and the confrontation line around Spicaste Stijena, Debelo Brdo, and Skenderija." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to move on to what happened on the 28th of August, the so-called Markale 2 incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you remember the incidents of the 28th of August and the shell that landed, where it landed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not one grenade. There were multiple grenades, and they landed near the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was asking about a shell that caused a number of casualties, fatalities. I'll ask you about all five of those, all five of the shells, of course, but I was just reminding you in a general way. As we go along, or "en passant," as they say in French, Mr. Dragomir Milosevic was wounded in the June and July offensive. He was absent throughout August because he was undergoing surgery in Belgrade and then treatment, and he simply wasn't there until the beginning of the shelling. Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor didn't ask anything about this event. Therefore, I have to dwell on it for a while, and I must admit I'm going to go into details. When I was reading your last statement, paragraph 25 from the document DD00-0319 -- paragraph 25, have you found it, sir? Do you have it in front of you, paragraph 25?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to read it out to you, the whole paragraph. "I believe that General Smith made the call to Pale and spoke with Mladic, but the call was made from my office because I had a direct line, and I was present to hear our end of the conversation." And then you go on to say: "When Mladic called back the next day, he did not specify what steps he had taken to investigate. He only stated that it had not been his forces who had done the shelling. I believe it was me, through my interpreter, who took that call from Mladic." So on the 29th you had this conversation. That's the day after. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in this conversation Mladic had pleaded for maximum effort to be made for this incident not to disrupt peace efforts that were being made in various quarters in the recent times, and that he was expecting the Muslims to allow for the possibility for a mixed commission, headed by General Smith, to review the whole incident and discover the truth about it? Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that he said something which was characteristic, that he wanted General Smith to be asked to bear in mind that for the same incident in Pale, a 20-millimetre shell was blamed as the cause of the incident; and then he ended that people were -- had people been in one barrel, in one place, it could not have caused such huge damage. Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember any details from this telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must tell you that I had serious problems regarding the document that's in my hands and in the hands of the OTP but of which we don't have a translation, and that's a transcript of the conversation which was recorded at 18:27 between General Ratko Mladic and an unidentified person from the office of the General Smith through Mladic's interpreter. This conversation took place at 1827 hours on the 28th of August, on the very day when the incident took place. I can present this, the whole document, but I am worried why there is no English translation for the OTP of this document. And I intend to tender this document into evidence, D00-0286. It has its OTP number, 03402152. In this regard, if possible, and with your leave, I would pose only two questions to General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, before you put those questions, could you just verify that this is another conversation other than the one you referred to just a while ago? I thought you said that the conversation in which you believed that the witness had taken part took place on the 29th of August, and the conversation that you're now going to ask about is a conversation which took place the day before, which is then a different conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. But that's the only, and only one, conversation that took place between the witness and the general. But in his statement, he claims that it took place on the 29th; however, this conversation took place on the 28th of August, at 1827 hours, unless the General may confirm that someone else talked from General Smith's office. And if that is the case, can he please tell us who this person was from General Smith's office who could have had this conversation. That's the whole point, Your Honours, because this document is self-explanatory. It's an official document, a transcript of the recorded conversation. It exists, and it was used in another case in which I didn't have time to go into it because that was not my job and I didn't investigate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if you have a proposition that you wish to put to this witness that derives from that document, you may put it and we'll hear his response.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My concern is that there is no translation of it into English in order to make it more clear. In front of me I only have the Serbian version. And this is such a hugely important document that I don't know how to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy that could be placed on the ELMO, and then it could be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's here in front of me. If the interpreters can translate it, then I'm going to propose it. It has its number, and I think that the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed by our case manager that an English translation may exist. If we could take a minute now to check that out, it may save five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please check that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had requested a translation into English several days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have an English version of this. I think we could e-mail it to the registrar, who could then put it on -- we couldn't put it directly into e-court from our terminal, but we could e-mail it to the registrar who, I think, could then do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whatever the technology allows, let us use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the witness to read it. While the witness is reading this, can a number be assigned to the video clip that we saw, please, for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I renew my objection to the receipt of that video clip, to the extent that the assignment of a number is the first step towards tendering it into evidence, on grounds of relevance, grounds of foundation, and untimely disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D26.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the question? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you read this document? Is that the conversation that you had with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not the conversation that I had with Mladic, but I can't exclude that this might be a transcription of a conversation between General Smith and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's even better. In any case, it happened on the 28th of August; is that correct? However, it says here that an unidentified person from General Smith's office had this conversation, and I wouldn't have asked you this at all had you not said in your October statement that as far as you can recall it was you who had this conversation. That is why -- otherwise, I wouldn't have asked you this. But if you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel just stated that the witness said in his October statement that it was he who had this conversation with General Mladic. I think that is a mischaracterisation of the record. The witness testified that he had a conversation with Ratko Mladic on the 29th of August. This document is dated the 28th of August, at 6.27 in the evening. This witness cannot authenticate this conversation on the record established so far. I do not preclude the possibility that further conversations may lay an adequate evidentiary basis for its admission; however, at this point I object to this witness being questioned concerning the contents of this document unless he can lay a foundation that he has knowledge of the contents of the document and that he is the person who participated in the conscious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're right about the -- I think he's right about the date. The counsel is right about the date, but as to whether the witness can speak to it is another matter, because he may know enough about the conversation. He doesn't rule out the possibility that it could have been with General Smith, but that seems unlikely to me because of the many references in the conversation to General Smith himself. So it would seem more likely to be a conversation with some person other than General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is precisely because what he said earlier. "It seems to me that I took this call with the help of the interpreter." This document explicitly says that this conversation took place through an interpreter and that General Smith had nothing to do with this conversation. That's what the witness said. So I must insist on this, that this conversation took place on the 28th, at 1827 hours. If he maintains that this conversation was made by General Smith, I have no further questions. I'm just questioning the issue that probably he made an error, that it did take place on the 28th, which is more logical, but my logic could be -- could be worthless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the witness again. What do you know about this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I remember, and that's how my witness testimony reads, is a phone conversation on 28 August in which General Smith asked General Mladic to investigate whether his troops had fired at the market in Sarajevo. And I also remember a conversation on 29 August in which General Mladic said that he had investigated the incident and that his troops were not to blame for the incident. What I can't exclude is that another phone conversation took place on 28 August, of which the text now appears on the ELMO, in which General Smith asked these questions. But I'm sorry to say that I can't state with certainty that I was present at that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may ask just one more question in this regard, and the witness can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from you, who could possibly be there, at such a crucial moment and at such an important time, in the office of General Smith?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could, for example, have been the military assistant, Colonel Baxter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about this. But can you tell us, on the evening of the 28th, was a decision made to use NATO to carry out strikes and for the purposes that it was used? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you something about that. That decision was taken only the day afterwards, on 29 August, when all data from the investigation of the market were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. That stands to reason, but I'm asking you something different. Was it decided on the 28th to carry out air-strikes? In order to set the NATO machinery in motion, it cannot be done in a matter of minutes. Certain conditions have to be fulfilled for NATO to be activated. It could not have acted on the very same evening. Everything was on standby. And orders to carry out the bombing were given on the evening of the 28th. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exclude that preparations were taken to deploy air power, but the decision to do so was definitely not taken on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue this matter any longer. Let me first ask you something about radar equipment. I would first like you to look at page 4 of the English version, paragraph 3 of the document DD00-0287. I repeat: Page 4, paragraph 3. You already said, and if you have it in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. It is impossible to do this more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you, sir? I said page 4, paragraph 3 of the document, the number of which I gave you. Can you see this? It begins with: "Our mortar radar detection equipment ..." "Our mortar radar detection equipment was not completely accurate in those early days, and we could not always say who was responsible for starting the incidents. Only when the Dutch equipment arrived later in 1995 did we have an accurate system." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 20 of the other statement, DD00-0311, paragraph 20 -- I'm not going to read the whole paragraph; it will take too much time. Do you have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence reads: "At the same time a British unit arrived also providing coverage over the city. The primary purpose of these radars was to locate the mortar and artillery positions of units firing into the city." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if it is true that neither the British nor the Dutch radars registered the shell that caused so many deaths and injuries? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that these radars failed to register the remaining four shells that you spoke of a minute ago? Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that neither the sound of the shell was registered? Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sound of the shots was not registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to continue my examination, let me first draw your attention again to the English version, page 4, but now we're going to deal with the last paragraph of the document DD00-0285. I have to read the whole passage to you, as soon as you have it in front of you. So page 4, English version, last paragraph, which is a rather long one. Do you have it in front of you? It begins with: "The most significant shelling in Sarajevo ..."

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you state this, sir: "The most significant shelling in Sarajevo occurred on the 28th of August between 11.10 and 11.20 when the marketplace was shelled. There were five shells fired that day, and one struck the roof of a building in the vicinity of the Markale marketplace. A rain of shrapnel came down on the marketplace." I will read on: "The first report was that more than 30 were killed and more than 40 injured. It was confirmed later that 33 were killed and more than 80 were injured. The chief UNMO and his staff went to the scene with an expert in analysing mortar explosions. A full investigation was ordered. We were very careful because of the implications for the London Conference, where such an act could bring about air-strikes. These air-strikes were significant as they meant not just calling for close-air support, C.A.S., but also for air-strikes on selected targets. "After 24 hours, on Tuesday, the 29th of August, we received the definitive report. The investigation confirmed that it was a 120-millimetre shell, and the direction was also confirmed. Our investigation with our men on the ground throughout the city, such as the UNMOs, confirmed that the firing had not been heard within the city itself and, therefore, it was highly probable the fire must have come from outside the confrontation line. "Based on my experience, I consider that someone would have heard the firing of the shells if they had been fired from within the confrontation lines. One can hear the difference between incoming and outgoing fire based on the sound. Even if it had been fired from the hills, it would have been heard. It is quite a loud bang. The Cymbelline had not picked it up either. All this indicates ..." Is that a correct statement, sir, what I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we have to go to paragraph 24 of DD00-0319, paragraph 24. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot yet confirm that. Now I do have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We've addressed this paragraph before, what Van Baal told you about. We heard that yesterday. I'm interested in the other half of the paragraph where you say no element -- you say: "Elements that were to be taken into account were always follows: If there was no sound to be heard, the shell must have been fired from far away." I think that's what it says. Can you please tell the Chamber, you say if it had been fired from a hill, the sound would have been heard. If that's what you're saying, if there was no shell, the shell would have been fired from far away, from beyond the hills, who knows from how far. Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, it means that the shells were not fired from the immediate vicinity of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not even from one of hills? Not from one of the hills?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hills start at the edge of the city but continue for quite a ways, so it depends. If it had happened within the immediate line of vision from the city, then I expect that the shots would have been heard; but if the distance was greater than that, then perhaps the shots could not be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a minute ago you said that the shots had not been heard, full stop. No sound of shots being fired, not within the area of responsibility of the BH army, or at least that's what you claimed a while ago. Well, after all, if you wish to add any further explanations, please, by all means, do so.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's all right. But then you go on to say, and this is what I'm interested in most of all, that the radars didn't clock that. And since the radars didn't clock that, you go on to say: "That means that the trajectory was exceptionally low." How is that possible - can you please explain? - that the radars failed to clock the shell; the trajectory had to be exceptionally low? We have a 120-millimetre shell. Can it have a linear trajectory and, as it were, keep flying up the radar all the time? In other words, can it go straight to the target, in a straight line? You are an expert yourself. In your opinion, if the shell kept flying under the radar, could it have kept a straight line all the way to the target? Can you please explain that, sir.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not possible. A mortar has an inclined trajectory, so a horizontal path is virtually out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The radars, as a matter of fact, did not clock the shell, which means that it was fired from somewhere inside the city, given what the facts are. Let's forget about the sound now. But the radars did nothing to clock this shell, and we're talking about state-of-the-art, cutting-edge radar technology, such as the British technology and the Dutch technology, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if the shells would have been fired from within the city, normally the radar would have clocked them, but the coverage of the radar may not have been 100 per cent. I do not have enough information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you - and I have to be very straightforward - is the explosion, this shell, whatever else, exploded in that very spot. That's what I'm putting to you. Have you an answer to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say about it is that the radar did not clock these shells. Unfortunately, that did not lead to any additional information. What I'm trying to say is that we had to go by the funnel analysis on the ground. The funnel analysis on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning everything that we have discussed, Witness, I have several questions for you now. We heard a while ago that a 120-millimetre shell hit the roof of a building and that a hail of shrapnel came down on the market. Is this something you heard from someone else, or were you actually there? Did you see this happen? Did you see this shell impacting, as it were?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I was at headquarters. This is the report of the analysis that took place. Four shells hit the ground, according to the report, and made a few casualties. One shell hit a building causing the shell to explode in the air, and the hail of shrapnel caused a lot of casualties. But I do not know this from my own observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: A question for clarification. General, the four shells you said hit the ground, did they hit the ground in the Markale market or in the vicinity of the market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They hit in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the fifth shell then hit a roof to a building adjacent, immediately adjacent, to the market; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, in the close vicinity of the market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So the casualties caused by that fifth shell were caused by the pieces of the roof and the shrapnel that fell down over the market; is that correct? Is that how it happened, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mainly the shrapnel from the shell. Because it explodes in mid-air, the effect is larger than when a shell hits the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, thank you. I was just about to try and clarify this very point. I'm talking about this one single shell. I'm asking the witness, and I'm adamant that I should, about the sound not being heard, about nothing being picked up by the radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about all five shells. None of them were picked up. I'm not merely saying this about the explosion, where it occurred. I'm talking about all the other explosions in that very spot where they occurred. That is what I'm putting to you, precisely because no sound was picked up and there were five shells. Five shells were fired, and indeed they were. It's in the indictment. How on earth is it possible for none of those shells to be picked up by the radar technology?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to ask, "What is the question?" But we just had it. How was it possible for none of those shells to be picked up by the radar technology? Are you able to answer that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you a final answer. It's a mystery to me as well. It is possible that the radar was not aimed in the right direction, but it's only conjecture. I can't give a final answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President, is that all that you wanted to ask the witness? Can I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wasn't asking the witness. I was trying to get you to ask a question. In future, just leave the introductory paragraphs out and get to the question as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He answered your question. He says it's a mystery to him. For the purposes of our Defence team, that answer is good enough. I won't be pushing him on this. You asked him. He said it's a mystery. Well, it's certainly a mystery to me as someone speaking on behalf of Mr. Milosevic's defence. I do want to ask the witness something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you see the footage that was seen by the entire world about the explosion, the people who were killed there, and the people who were injured? Did you see that footage, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about a shell hitting a roof and the shrapnel coming down? You saw the photographs; right? Can it possibly cause the type of injury that was seen there? I'm not going into that. I think I'm losing a lot of time. Can that sort of thing cause the sort of injury that is seen in the footage? If you're unable to answer, sir, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very well possible to cause this damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're an artilleryman, aren't you? You must know, then, that if we have mortar shells of that calibre, it's very difficult to determine the position that these are fired from, since it's impossible to determine the charge that was used in order to fire that sort of a missile. As an artilleryman, do you know this for a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know it's not simple to conduct a funnel analysis. I couldn't even do it myself. But experts can get lots of information from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But are you at least aware of this fact: Is it at all possible to determine that, given what I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's absolutely possible. You can determine the direction from where the shelling came, and within a certain margin you can also estimate from what distance the shell must have been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, had you provided a different answer, I probably wouldn't have asked the question, anyway. But did you know about this highly classified document drafted by General Janvier and submitted to the Secretary-General Kofi Annan personally on the 28th, as early as the 28th of August? Can you please look at the whole paragraph so that I don't have to show anything to you. This is 65 ter document 481. The English page is 3, page 3. I will not be reading that for you. I could show you the important part. If not, perhaps you can just go ahead and read this silently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I show the witness the relevant portion, or does the Chamber want the witness to go through the entire document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Show him the relevant portions. If it becomes necessary, he can then look at the entire passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, sir? All right. I'll read this -- I've read it, as a matter of fact. You've answered. But I'll do it again. It's a highly confidential report dated the 28th. First of all, were you aware of this report, sir, that same day? This one. Did you ever become aware of this, where it reads: "In the case of mortar shells, it is very difficult to determine" - it's about the 120-millimetre mortar shells - "where they are fired from as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectile." The afternoon of the 28th of August. How would you answer that question in the light of your previous answers, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take the time to read this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We also need to read it. Have you completed the reading? Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, I want to see what the witness has to say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it impossible, what it says here, or is it different?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I read here seems to be a situation report dated 28 August. At any rate, it describes the incident that took place and that investigations are being conducted to find the point of origin, the firing point of origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put your question again, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have to go back to what I was asking. I didn't expect just to dwell on this for this long. This is quite contrary to what the witness statement a while ago, but here, it's in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "For mortar rounds it is very difficult to determine the firing positions as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles. The afternoon of the 28th of August." Is it correct, what the report suggests, that it is impossible to determine this, or is it not impossible? Is the case what you just explained to us a while ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to Mr. Tapuskovic's misquoting this document and the question he is putting to the witness. The document does not say it is impossible. The document says it is "very difficult."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, but it goes on to say, "... as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles." Let me read it in its entirety. It says: "The definition of firing positions for mortar rounds is very difficult, as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles." That is what the witness should comment on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that it is very difficult to determine the calibre and the firing point. I cannot confirm that it is impossible. During the whole period that I was on mission crater analyses were made several times, sometimes with success and sometimes with less success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it then that you don't agree with the statement that it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. In some cases it is very well possible to determine the charge, the level of charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In fact, it seems to me that there is a sort of contradiction, speaking as a layperson, because a difficulty doesn't create an impossibility, it creates a difficulty. But the conclusion that it is impossible to determine the level of charge is not consistent with the previous proposition that the definition of firing positions is very difficult. It appears, to me, to be a slight contradiction between "difficulty" and "impossibility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. Can I perhaps try and approach this from a slightly different perspective? Because it would seem to me, and, General, please correct me if I'm wrong, that the determination of the firing point and the level of charge used to fire a mortar is possible when you have a crater, so you can do a crater analysis. But in this case, we understand there is no crater because the shell hit the roof of the building just next to the market, and most of the damage caused was caused by the things that fell down from the roof, including the shrapnel from the grenade itself. So what I'm interested in is more the words included in the report just before the passage that the President has read out, namely that "the mortar shell was assessed to be fired from 170-degrees magnetic." Because that might be more helpful to determine at least which direction the mortar came from. So can you enlighten us how the determination of the 170 degrees was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour is right. The shell that hit the building could not be investigated, so the analysis was done on the craters of the remaining four shells. When the investigations were concluded on August 29, the expert was certain in stating that the shells had been fired from a south/south-west direction and that they had been fired from a distance between 3.5 and 4.5 kilometres. That is what I remember and what was being told at the briefing based on the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, that is the right subject, and what you have just broached is a subject that will prominent later on. The shell had a crater. It had a crater, but it didn't hit the roof. But I'm not going into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, do you know that the shelling was stopped for a day, that the Russian officer Demurenko was in charge of that whole area? He said it was one chance in a million that the shell had come from Serb positions, and he said the crater could have been what it was only had the shell fallen straight down from the sky. And then his estimate was one in a million in terms of the chances for a shell to have been fired from the Serb positions. Has a crater been found? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the lengthy testimony that counsel is giving before he puts a question to the witness. Mr. Demurenko is not on the stand; Mr. Nicolai is. Mr. Nicolai should be asked questions without these several sentences of prefatory material concerning counsel's view of the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I've already spoken to Mr. Tapuskovic about these lengthy introductions. Get to the point quickly without the introductions. I find that it is in order for him to put to the witness what Mr. Demurenko said and to get his views on this technical matter. We are, however, well past the time for the adjournment, and we are going to adjourn now. When we return, we'll get back to this question. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, how much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to skip a few things concerning Markale, and there's another topic I will deal with. Hopefully I will finish very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And remember, just get to the point. Ask the question without all the prefatory, the introductory, remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going to mention -- I wouldn't have mentioned Mr. Demurenko had there not been mention of the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, there you go again. Just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does the witness know that NATO bombings were suspended for a day because the chief of the sector where what we are talking about took place claimed publicly that it was impossible to hit the Serbian positions? A crater had been found, and he spoke about the chance of one in a million. In other words, it meant that the shell could only have arrived in a straight line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That it could have landed - I'm using very simple terms - as if it had arrived from the sky?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any of that. As far as I know, the air-strikes continued throughout the week, the entire week, and I don't remember any report from Mr. Demurenko regarding a likelihood of one in a million that the mortars would not have been fired from the Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, the report sent by General Janvier on the 28th was sent directly to Kofi Annan in light of the significance of the whole affair, and words were carefully chosen concerning qualifications and characteristics of a 120-millimetre shell. So this had been checked. So if such a report was sent directly to the UN in view of the importance of the whole affair, due care was taken of what was put in that report.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on what basis General Janvier sent this report to Mr. Kofi Annan. The outcome of the investigation was reported to the staff only on 29 August. So I can't imagine on what General Janvier could have based this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you didn't know anything about that report?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please take a look at document DD00-0287. Page 5, paragraph 3. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It begins with "We were surprised ..." with these words, "We were surprised ..." Before I read it out to you, negotiations were underway at the time about peaceful solutions, and they were progressing well in the aftermath of the Srebrenica events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me read what it says here: "We were surprised at the timing of this incident after the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa and during the quiet months of August when we were checking with the Bosnian Serbs. We felt that we were making some progress with the negotiations. I am therefore of the opinion that perhaps Mladic did not order the firing of the shells ..." And maybe I can read on, if necessary, but you can also read it for yourself. But I would like to hear from you whether what you wrote here is correct.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that this was not necessary at all for the Serbian side, in view of everything that had happened at that time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's difficult for me to answer. Perhaps it's even impossible for me to answer. It was cause to conduct a very thorough investigation and not to exclude any possibility as to the perpetrators. And only once the report had been completed on the 29th and the investigators stated that there was a 99 per cent certainty that the shells had been fired from Serb area, only then did we take additional steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question about the Markale incident is as follows: The BH army had both political and military reasons for the negotiations to fail and collapse and for the army of Republika Srpska to capitulate and be defeated. Is it fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are assumptions. All I can have an opinion about is facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that fit with what Van Baal had told you, that if the highest interest of a state, then their own people can be used as an instrument for that, and to victimise it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an option that we did not exclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question, but for the record, I note a mischaracterisation of the testimony regarding Major General Van Baal. That is not what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this has been confirmed by this witness, that they didn't rule out that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last topic is that this was followed by NATO bombardment, and I wouldn't dwell too long on that. I should move now again to the document that you have in front of you, but let's move on to page 7, paragraph 3. Do you have it in front of you, sir? The paragraph begins, "On the 23rd of May ..." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "On the 23rd of May, the Bosnian Serbs removed some heavy weapons from a weapon collection point." I believe I have no reason to go on. If the witness would like me to do that, I have no objection. Is it true that this is what happened?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that already at that time NATO had bombed the ammunition depot in Pale, as you mention further on, which was situated in a residential area? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that these NATO bombs -- and I heard a lot about them and read about that. I'm not a military expert, but I learned and heard from other people that these NATO bombs do not only create damage at the place of impact, but people get injured and disintegrated in the very wide area due to the blast of the impact. Is that correct? Even if the target was directly engaged, civilians nevertheless got killed in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, is this relevant to any of the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was precisely the result that was to bring about certain reactions from the other side and for certain steps to be taken that would deteriorate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, on the 25th of May, two days later, there was another bombing, and it says: "Mladic accused us of hitting a hospital and a school, to which we responded that an ammunition depot is a rather -- an odd place to have a hospital." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will allow the question, but bear in mind that NATO is not on trial here, and it doesn't help your case merely to cite bombings by NATO unless they relate to allegations in the indictment. Let's have the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can state about this matter is that only on 25 and 26 May were NATO bombing attacks carried out, and they targeted a munitions complex outside Pale and that the targets were hit. How many victims there were and whether they were military or civilians I cannot tell you because I do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain to Your Honours, in response to your question, how relevant this is. The indictment says that throughout the whole period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have allowed the question. Move on. We must be concluding your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The bombs that were dropped on the Serbian positions, it wasn't only the Serbian side that, in the period of your tour of duty, used these air bombs. The Serbian positions were also struck by aerial bombs fired by NATO in the last three months, and they caused equal damage as the one caused -- as alleged in the indictment by the air bombs fired by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand any part of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another question, Mr. Tapuskovic. And you must be bringing your cross-examination to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm almost finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did NATO ever issue written orders, in case of retaliation or for pressing military reasons, to undertake such actions?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The UN resolutions indicate, including Resolution 824 of the UN, indicates that air force can be used in defending these areas, including safe ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And finally two more questions. After all these bombardments by NATO on the 23rd, the 25th of May, and after the intervention, so after all these bombings - I had a paper in front of the microphone so you may not have heard me - was all this that had to be done about the bombing referred to the UN? Because prior to that everything was done single-handedly by NATO. So after that everything was moved to New York.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I repeat that air-strikes were carried out only on 25 and 26 May, not on 23rd May. The air-strikes were, indeed, carried out by aircraft of NATO but at the request and under the responsibility of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After you have completed your mission in Bosnia on the 2nd of September, do you know that in September, October, and November the army of Republika Srpska was compelled to defend itself both from NATO bombs and from the attacks by the BH army, and that actually everything it did, it did only as a defence, in the three months that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some problems with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. Mr. Docherty, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've terminated the cross-examination. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major General --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major General, during his cross-examination Mr. Tapuskovic asked you about a quotation from your statement of 13 November 1995; "Every man and boy had a weapon." First of all, do you remember being questioned about that by Mr. Tapuskovic, or actually being asked several questions about that by Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: For the sake of completeness, I wish to ask you a question or two which Mr. Tapuskovic did not ask you concerning a subsequent written clarification of that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, may we please see pages with ERN numbers 06046776 and the following page, 06046777.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could I have the number for document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There appears to be some difficulty finding the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I show the document to the registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Anything to get matters moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. And may I ask, could we scroll down so we could see paragraph 30, 3-0, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major General, do you see paragraph 30 in front of you in English, left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you read it to yourself, please. It continues on the next page, so just let us know when you're ready for the next page.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can scroll down to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Have you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now that you've read it, can you tell the Court what effect you were trying to achieve when you used that phrase originally, "Every man and boy had a weapon"?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. To put an end to sniping, we dealt with the authorities of the parties concerned, assuming that they wielded control over the military people under their command. This did not provide a hundred per cent guarantee that the sniping incidents could be put to a stop, because a lot of civilians had weapons as well and controlling the civilians was far more difficult. Nonetheless, I believe that if all authorities cooperated, the number of sniping incidents would have been reduced considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were also asked -- excuse me. You were also asked - I'm shifting topics here - about allegations of the Bosnians firing on their own people. Again, do you remember that exchange between you and Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When General Van Baal and you had this conversation, did General Van Baal tell you about one occasion or more than one occasion on which he thought this might have occurred?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did General Van Baal tell you the basis of his assertion? Did he see this himself, or had he heard this from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me about -- also about sniping in the centre of Sarajevo where, during his tour of duty, was responsible for that sniping incident, and it was seriously suspected that the incident had been caused by Bosnian Muslims, the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But to answer the question, was General Van Baal basing this upon material he had received from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer was based on the outcome of investigations into the incident that happened during the period that he was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Switching topics again. There were -- oh, excuse me. One last question. When did General Van Baal leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was mid-1994. He was Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR in the first half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions concerning the shelling of the Markale market on 28 August 1995. Did you personally participate in any of the investigations that were conducted into that shelling?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you go to the -- how long after the shelling was it before you went to the marketplace yourself, if indeed you went?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was two or three days after the shooting incident. Excuse me, the shelling incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And up until then, where had you been?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were asked some questions by Mr. Tapuskovic concerning rogue elements, and again there was a quotation from one statement. Do you remember being asked that by Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, again, for the sake of completeness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, could we go to the preceding page, please, ERN 06046776, and display paragraph 26 on screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, would you please -- do you have paragraph 26 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you please read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you stand by your statement that the Bosnian Serb army was very disciplined? Do you --

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreter. Do you stand by your statement that somebody in that army gave the order to fire those shells?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The last topic I want to cover is the issue of provocation and response that we covered yesterday. As a military officer with 39 years of experience, does the phrase "counter-battery fire" have a specific professional meaning to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Please tell the Chamber what a professional military officer means by "counter-battery fire."

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counter-battery fire is resulting fire at an unknown target that has been fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me ask this: What does the phrase "battery" in that -- what's the "battery" that we're referring to that's being countered?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A battery is a firing unit comprising multiple pieces of artillery and is comparable to a company within the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what is the point of counter-battery fire? What is a military commander hoping to achieve when he orders that counter-battery fire be directed upon a particular position?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of counter-battery fire is to neutralise the firing unit that one -- by which one was fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, let's apply those principles in a few questions to the situation in Sarajevo. You described that some of the fire directed onto the city of Sarajevo appeared to you to have been provoked by the Bosnians. Is that an accurate summary of the testimony you gave?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you observe the Bosnians to be firing in order to be provocative?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I need to be a bit more precise there. Only once did I personally observe shooting, so most of my information comes from UNMOs and from military people who were part of UNPROFOR. I personally experienced shelling from the BiH barracks at the ice stadium, and I experienced that from near our headquarters. Open -- there was shelling from open-roofed vehicles towards Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you recall on about how many occasions were you informed by your colleagues in UNPROFOR about BiH shelling? You said you only saw it once, but you received information from military people in UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exact number of shelling incidents of this type I don't remember, but there were definitely more than 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And about how many rounds were fired by the Bosnians in a typical act of provocation?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes only one shot; other times, two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, where he would have had this -- would this have been part of the information he received, or are you talking about the single incident that he witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I was asking a question about "typical," Your Honour, by which I meant -- I thought that by clarifying the basis of his knowledge, one personal observation, plus 10 or so reports received, I thought that he was qualified to answer a question that asked for a typical act of provocation, and that's why I phrased it the way I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let's hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some cases, only one shot was fired. In any case, the incident near the UNPROFOR headquarters involved only one shot. The case that took place at the BiH barracks involved a few shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: With what type of weapons? What type of weapons did the Bosnians fire?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shells. In the case of the vehicle, a light calibre. A heavy calibre wouldn't fit in the vehicle without causing damage. In the case of the BH barracks, there were only mortars, but I don't know their calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I want to talk to you now about the scale of response to these acts of provocation. Did what you observed, in the case of something you saw yourself, or what you read about, in the case of reports received, fit into what you, as a military officer, would describe as counter-battery fire, which I believe you've testified is fire intended to take out the source from which one is being fired upon?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, the fire was returned in the direction from which firing had come. In other cases, this did not happen and the retaliation consisted of arbitrary firing at the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In the case -- first of all, let's get some numbers, if we can. You've testified to seeing one incident yourself, and I believe you said approximately 10 that you read about. First of all, do I have my numbers right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so of these total 11 incidents, how many times was the response counter-battery fire; how many times was the response, to use your word, arbitrary?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have that answer. Could you repeat it so we can have it interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my regret, I cannot give an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Then let me ask: In the times that the response was arbitrary, however many times that was, what sorts of weapons were used in response by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this means mortars and artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were these modified air bombs that you testified about yesterday ever used? Before you answer, Mr. Tapuskovic has something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the Prosecutor, my learned colleague, to show us where did he say that it was the Serbs who fired random shots? He spoke about the BH army firing randomly in order for the Serbian forces to respond with a few shells in order to neutralise the firing points. I do not remember, but can my learned colleague show me where is it that the witness said this in any part of his testimony? Maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I believe he has testified to that. I couldn't cite a transcript page, but I'm happy to clear that up with a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.
